..
Issued at 405 AM CDT Wed Sep 16 2026

An upper level low pressure system will move into the Northern
High Plains this weekend and then linger over the area into
early next week. A lot of uncertainty remains in the evolution
of this system but currently it looks like western and southern
portions of the forecast area will be favored for precipitation.

Until it arrives we will see a couple of precipitation chances.
The first being during the day today in an area of strong warm
advection ahead of an inverted trough over southern portions of
the area, and with a northern stream shortwave tracking across
southern Canada.

Currently, shower activity is noted over north central Montana
and into southern Saskatchewan, associated with the northern
stream wave. To our south, mid and high level clouds are
increasing over eastern Wyoming into western South Dakota ahead
of an approaching wave. A surface low presently over central
Wyoming will lift into northeast Wyoming by around 18 UTC with
an inverted trough northward along the MT/ND border. Strong warm
advection with an increasing Southeast flow will result in 
strong moisture transport into the forecast area, with showers 
developing over south central ND late morning to early 
afternoon and spreading north and east through the day. This 
activity looks to be isolated to scattered in nature, especially
early on. Later this afternoon, as the strong moisture 
transport lifts well into northern ND, there may be some 
enhancement in shower activity as the increasing moisture 
interacts with the aforementioned Canadian shortwave. NBM 
depicts increasing precipitation chances through the afternoon 
as activity lifts north and east, with an area of likely pops 
near the Turtle Mountains by mid to late afternoon. 
Precipitation with this system today is expected to be light, 
mainly trace amounts to a tenth of an inch or so, especially 
early on. The potential for higher amounts, to maybe a quarter 
inch, increase later today from the James River Valley into the 
Turtle Mountains area. And finally, the potential for thunder is
low, but there is a decent amount of elevated instability 
situated around the JRV. If there's an area where the warm 
advection is strong enough, some elevated convection would be 
possible. This could yield some locally higher precipitation 
amounts. There is also enough dry air around that if we don't 
see strong enough warm advection to produce elevated convection,
we may just end up with our lower amounts of a trace to maybe a
tenth of an inch.

Precipitation lifts north and east of the forecast area early 
this evening and high pressure builds over southern Canada and
into northern North Dakota. There are a couple of scenarios for
tonight into Thursday morning. The first being a potential for
frost across northern North Dakota. Currently the northwest and
far north central look to be the favored areas. Another scenario
would be low stratus and fog over the area, limiting the
potential for frost. There is a signal for low stratus and fog 
in both the RAP and HRRR. Bufkit RAP/HRRR/NAM soundings indicate
the potential for stratus/fog tonight, but not so much from the
GFS. The latest NBM is depicting around a 15-30 percent
probability for MVFR ceilings Thursday morning, with even lower
probabilities for IFR conditions. I would suspect we may see by
late this afternoon or early evening if this would occur by
noting the amount of lower clouds over southern Canada within
the convergence zone north of the forecast area. Tonight as the
aforementioned inverted trough tracks east, northernly surface
flow will spread south allowing the lower stratus to drop south
across the forecast area. Farther south, over southern portions
of the forecast area, we could see a little better chance of 
fog, with less clouds initially and better radiational cooling. 
As high pressure builds over the area by Thursday morning, the 
far north may clear out anyway, with stratus early, then a few 
hours of cold temperatures early Thursday morning. Will need to 
monitor for the potential of a Frost Advisory, but at this time 
there it too much uncertainty.

The next wave tracks across southern portions of the area
Thursday evening into Friday morning. The general consensus is 
that the majority of the heavier rain will remain south of the 
state. However, there has been a bit of a northward shift in
qpf. Currently the NBM indicates generally a quarter to three 
quarters of an inch of qpf from 06Z-18Z Friday, so late Thursday
night through Friday morning over far south central ND into the
southern JRV. This tapers to around 0.05" to 0.15" from 
Bismarck to Jamestown. thus, higher amounts are favored along 
the far southern tier counties, from eastern Sioux and Emmons 
into Dickey and LaMoure Counties. Little if any precip is 
expected from southwest into north central ND. There is another 
area of light qpf (under a tenth of an inch) noted from west 
central into northwest ND.
